definition: Involved with others in something wrong, even if only by helping quietly or staying silent.
example: By ignoring the fake reviews on the bakery's website, the manager became complicit in the deception.
nuance: Complicit means sharing the guilt for a wrong; compliant just means obedient, and complacent means smugly unconcerned.
prompt: A student learns that a friend plans to copy answers during a quiz.
options: Lending her answer sheet made the student complicit in the cheating.
The student was complicit with the teacher's rules and turned in her quiz on time.
By reporting the plan to the teacher, the student made herself complicit in it.
The quiz was so complicit that nobody finished the last page.
reasons: Knowingly helping a friend cheat makes her share in the wrongdoing.
Following rules is being compliant; there is no wrongdoing to share here.
Exposing a wrong is the opposite of taking part in it.
This confuses the word with complicated; a quiz cannot share guilt.

practice.prompt: Club members discover their treasurer has been spending dues on personal snacks.
options: Members who saw the receipts and stayed silent were complicit in the misuse.
Pleased with last year's success, the club grew complicit and stopped recruiting.
The member who first questioned the spending was the most complicit of all.
The club thanked its complicit volunteers for running a wonderful spring bake sale.
reasons: Knowing about the wrong and keeping quiet lets it continue, so they share the blame.
Lazy self-satisfaction is complacency, not involvement in a wrong.
Challenging the misuse of money is the opposite of going along with it.
The word carries guilt, so it can't be used to praise helpful volunteers.
